newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ING seen eyeing Belgium for next move.
newsitem.headline: ING seen eyeing Belgium for next move.

text.p: Belgium could be next in the firing line as speculation resurfaces about where ING Groep will focus its acquisition sights in the wake of its latest move in the United States.
The Dutch financial services group last week achieved the first of its expansion priorities with the $2.2 billion agreed bid for Equitable of Iowa Companies.
But barely had the ink dried on this deal before analysts were assessing how ING would meet its goal of beefing up its European corporate banking activities.

Analysts see a range of options for ING, which recently changed its strategy by indicating an interest in lifting its presence in European banking, particularly Germany and France, ahead of the introduction of a single currency.
The banking and insurance company acknowledged at a news conference last week that its expansion opportunities on the continent lay outside its small home market.

Deputy chairman Godfried van der Lugt said ING had "done all of the mergers and acquisitions" it needed in the Netherlands. "The money we have left doesn't have to be invested in expansion (in the Netherlands), only in organic growth," he said.
He said expansion in Europe could involve Belgium as well as Germany and France.
"The problem is that in Europe, very few companies are on sale and, if they are, the prices are very high," van der Lugt told reporters.
He said medium-sized companies were not prepared to give up their independence, particularly to a foreign player.
"Don't be surprised if in the next few years we might do something in banking but I don't think we will be playing a (big) part," he said.

Andrew Goodwin of UBS said ING's 20 percent stake in Belgium's Bank Brussels Lambert (BBL) may play a part in its next move. The stake is a remnant of ING's attempt to take the Belgium bank over in the early 1990s.
Bart van der Feen of IRIS said: "I think BBL is still interesting for ING."
He expected a merger, takeover or some form of cooperation involving ING and BBL by the end of 1998 or 1999.
But he said the German and French markets were less interesting as it was difficult to buy a bank of good quality.
Kempen and Co analyst Hans Pluijgers saw opportunities for ING in Blegium banking and insurance, including insurer Royale Belge, which owns 12.4 percent of BBL.
"I suspect something is going to happen there," he said, adding however it was unclear if Belgium would welcome a foreign takeover.
He also saw an opportunity to buy another commercial bank in eastern Europe as former communist countries continued their privatisation drive. ING already controls Poland's Bank Slaski.
But Pluijgers said Germany and France were not good markets in which to make big acquisitions.
"There are no opportunities in my opinion. I expect ING to look at smaller niche players in the near future," he said.
Paribas analyst Tom Bennett noted that although banks in Europe were cheaper than insurers, few were for sale.
He did not expect ING to make acquisitions which would dilute shareholders' equity in the long term.
"My present feeling is that you will not see very much in the short term. I can't believe there's much available at the right price," Bennett said.
ING has a policy that acquisitions must earn a net return on capital invested of at least 11 percent.
Bennett also believed it was possible ING could do something with BBL, around which rumours have swirled for a long time including that it would merge with another Belgium bank.
But another analyst said: "That's a complicated and messy situation."
The analyst said Belgium banking was an area for expansion but it was "in a fix" while the European banking sector was 10 years behind the insurance sector in terms of rationalisation.
